title: Prodigal delegate returns, Leonard retires, Moore stocks the bench, more, in political notes
summary: Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat is interested in legislating again, Dels. Jheanelle Wilkins and Karen Toles have roles in National Black Caucus of State Legislators, PSC spokesperson steps away and four new district judges take the bench, in political notes.
content:
by Christine Condon, William J. Ford and Steve Crane, Maryland Matters July 15, 2026

by Christine Condon, William J. Ford and Steve Crane, Maryland Matters July 15, 2026

Del. Christopher Eric Bouchat (R-Frederick and Carroll) famously washed his hands of the General Assembly this spring, refusing to participate in committee or floor sessions in what he called a protest of Republicans’ lack of clout in the legislature.

From late February through the end of the legislative session, Bouchat would show up on most mornings that the House was in session, register his presence, then turn around and drive to his business in Arbutus for the rest of the day.

That was then. This is now.

With the General Assembly scheduled to meet for a special session next month to consider a possible constitutional amendment dealing with congressional redistricting, Bouchat is suddenly interested in legislating again. In separate emails over the last several weeks, Bouchat said he would reintroduce a redistricting bill that failed this year — then expressed disappointment at the fact that other legislation was not likely to be taken up, as is the custom during special sessions.

“If redistricting is important enough to warrant a special session, then serious reform proposals should be heard,” Bouchat said of his proposal for a Citizen Redistricting Convention.

That proposal is based on Bouchat’s House Bill 56, which called for creation of a 188-member body of citizens that would be elected every 10 years to set legislative and congressional district boundaries after each decennial census. That bill was sent to the House Rules and Executive Nominations Committee, where it died without a hearing.

Bouchat, who resisted calls to resign during the legislative session, and faced a resolution for expulsion that went nowhere, did not run for reelection this year. He is finishing his first four-year term in the House.

Tori Leonard, a longtime spokesperson for the commission that regulates public utilities in Maryland, retired earlier this month, after a lengthy career serving in communications roles at various state agencies.

Leonard spent nearly 11 years as director of communications at the Public Service Commission, according to the commission. While she started her career in radio news, including a stint as a news anchor and reporter for WBAL News Radio in Baltimore, Leonard went on to serve in communications roles for the Maryland Department of Health, Maryland Insurance Administration, Maryland Department of Business and Economic Development and Baltimore County government, the commission said.

The commission has already selected a new director, said spokesperson Kathy Fueston, and will likely issue an announcement next week.

Two Maryland legislators are helping to craft policy on education and criminal justice reform as part of the National Black Caucus of State Legislators, which will meet in Philadelphia in December.

Dels. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) and Karen Toles (D-Prince George’s) serve on two of the 10 legislative policy committees that met virtually last month to share state-level policy updates and review emerging trends.

Wilkins, vice chair of the caucus’ education committee, serves as chair of the House Ways and Means Committee in Annapolis, which handles education, among other subjects. Ways and Means reviewed several early childhood education bills this year, such as the state’s popular child care scholarship program.

Toles serves as chair of the caucus’ law, justice and ethics committee. In Annapolis, she had served on the House Judiciary Committee, which crafts policy on public safety, juvenile justice and the judiciary, before being shifted this year to the House Appropriations Committee.

According to a caucus newsletter distributed Tuesday, the education committee discussed a variety of topics such as state-sponsored universal pre-K programs, public education funding and school consolidation “as a possible way for students in smaller schools to gain access to better facilities.”

Part of the discussion with the national caucus’ Law, Justice and Ethics Committee dealt with mid-decade redistricting efforts that the newletter said would “dilute Black political power and representation at both the state and federal levels.” The Maryland General Assembly plans to hold special session Aug. 3-5 on congressional redistricting.

The caucus ethics committee also discussed the U.S. Supreme Court’s Callais ruling that gutted racial protections in the 1965 Voting Rights Act. Anticipating that ruling, Maryland this year passed its own version of the Voting Rights Act. joining eight other states that enacted statewide voting rights legislation.

Gov. Wes Moore last week announced four new district court judges, to fill vacancies on the bench in Allegany, Anne Arundel and Charles counties.

In Anne Arundel County, Deputy State’s Attorney Brian Anthony Marsh, a former assistant attorney general in the Medicaid fraud unit, will be heading to the bench. Marsh also worked as an assistant state’s attorney in the Baltimore City Special Victim’s Unit, where he prosecuted cases involving human trafficking, sex offenses and technology-facilitated crimes against children. He earned his law degree from the Columbus School of Law at the Catholic University of America.

He will be joined on the Anne Arundel County bench by Windy Rhea Ortega, an attorney in private practice who has her own firm, handling a wide range of adult and juvenile clients. Before that she was of counsel for Parker, Pallett, Slezak & Russell, litigating personal injury and wrongful death suits. The governor’s announcement of her appointment says she is highly skilled in constitutional and evidentiary litigation. Ortega earned her law degree from the Charlotte School of Law.

Jessica Lynne Colwell, a public defender for 25 years, has been named district judge in Allegany County, where she serves as public defender for Allegany and Garrett counties. She spent 15 years as a public defender in Baltimore City, 12 of those in the felony trial division. After working as the supervising attorney in the Garrett County Public Defender’s Office, she became deputy district public defender for Allegany and Garrett in 2018, and assumed her current role in 2021. She is a graduate of the University of Maryland School of Law.

Elizabeth Dorothy Theobalds will join the district court in Charles County, where she began her law career with the Charles County State’s Attorney’s Office, handling criminal matters and supervising the Child Support Division. She joined the County Attorney’s Office in 2008 and has been deputy county attorney since 2011, continuing her practice in land use, zoning and local government law. She earned her law degree from the University of Baltimore School of Law and an MBA from the university’s Robert G. Merrick School of Business, and has taught at the University of Maryland, University College and the College of Southern Maryland.

— This story was updated on Thursday, July 16, to correct the time and place of the National Black Caucus of State Legislators meeting, and Del. Karen Toles’ committee assignment.
